steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper on optimal reference translations: why standard references are no longer good enough for evaluating strong MT, what we propose, the research questions and contributions, and an outline of the rest of the paper.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Machine translation (MT) is usually evaluated with various segment-level similarity metrics against one or more reference translations. But reference translations obtained in the standard way are often criticized because they have flaws of various kinds. For several high-resourced language pairs the quality of MT gets to levels comparable to the quality of the reference translation, and sometimes MT is even significantly better than humans in a particular evaluation setting. From this one could conclude that state-of-the-art MT has got to a point where reference-based evaluation is not reliable anymore, and that we have to use other methods (like targeted expert evaluation of particular outputs), even though they are costly, subjective and maybe impossible to automate.

The narrow goal of this work is to make an ‘‘extension of the expiry date’’ possible for reference-based evaluation methods. More broadly, we want to formulate a methodology for creating reference translations that avoid the deficiencies often seen in ‘‘standard’’ or ‘‘professional’’ reference translations. These can be multiple interfering phenomena, inappropriate expressions, ignoring topic-focus articulation (information structure) or other abundant shortcomings in the translation, which show that the authors are insensitive to the topic itself, but most of all to the source and target language. For this we introduce so-called optimal reference translations (ORT), which are meant to represent optimal (ideal or excellent) human translations (if they were the subject of a translation quality evaluation). We focus on document-level translation and evaluation, which fits current trends in MT research and also this special issue of NLE. We hope that ORT will be a new approach to evaluating excellent MT outputs by becoming a gold standard in the true sense of the word. The questions our work deals with are:

- Questions
  - how to navigate MT research where MT quality already very good?
  - worth creating expensive ORT to compare with MT?
  - will various annotator groups recognize the quality difference between ORT and standard translations?

- Contributions
  - definition of ORT; analysis of evaluations; evaluation vs translation editing
  - what high-quality translation means for different annotator types
  - Optimal Reference Translations of English \rightarrow Czech dataset, subset evaluated

- Outline
  - related work (Section 2); ORT definition and creation (Section 3)
  - evaluation campaign: data, interface, instructions (Section 3.2)
  - statistics; predicting human ratings (Overall from Spelling, Style, Meaning...) with automated metrics (Section 4); document-level from segment-level
  - qualitative analysis (Section 5); broader discussion of human evaluation (Section 6)
  - code and data public

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Machine translation (MT) is usually evaluated with various segment-level similarity metrics against one or more reference translations. But reference translations obtained in the standard way are often criticized because they have flaws of various kinds. For several high-resourced language pairs the quality of MT gets to levels comparable to the quality of the reference translation, and sometimes MT is even significantly better than humans in a particular evaluation setting. From this one could conclude that state-of-the-art MT has got to a point where reference-based evaluation is not reliable anymore, and that we have to use other methods (like targeted expert evaluation of particular outputs), even though they are costly, subjective and maybe impossible to automate.

The narrow goal of this work is to make an ‘‘extension of the expiry date’’ possible for reference-based evaluation methods. More broadly, we want to formulate a methodology for creating reference translations that avoid the deficiencies often seen in ‘‘standard’’ or ‘‘professional’’ reference translations. These can be multiple interfering phenomena, inappropriate expressions, ignoring topic-focus articulation (information structure) or other abundant shortcomings in the translation, which show that the authors are insensitive to the topic itself, but most of all to the source and target language. For this we introduce so-called optimal reference translations (ORT), which are meant to represent optimal (ideal or excellent) human translations (if they were the subject of a translation quality evaluation). We focus on document-level translation and evaluation, which fits current trends in MT research and also this special issue of NLE. We hope that ORT will be a new approach to evaluating excellent MT outputs by becoming a gold standard in the true sense of the word. The questions our work deals with are:

- How should future MT research be navigated for languages where the quality of MT is already very good?

- Is it worth it to create an expensive optimal reference translation to compare MT with?

- If different groups of annotators evaluate optimal reference translations and standard translations, will all of them recognize the difference in quality?

Our contributions are then:

- a definition of optimal reference translation and an in-depth analysis of evaluations and of the relationship between evaluation and translation editing;

- a reflection on what a high-quality translation means for different types of annotators;

- publication of the Optimal Reference Translations of English \rightarrow Czech dataset, with a subset evaluated in the way described above.

First we discuss related work (Section 2), then we define ORT and describe how it was created (Section 3). After that we describe our evaluation campaign of ORT, with the data, the annotation interface and the annotation instructions (Section 3.2). Then we look at our data from a statistical perspective and measure how predictable the human ratings are (e.g. Overall rating from Spelling, Style, Meaning, etc.) using automated metrics (Section 4). We pay special attention to predicting the document-level rating from the segment-level. In Section 5, the penultimate one, we give a detailed qualitative analysis of the human annotations, and then we discuss this work in the bigger perspective of human evaluation of translations (Section 6). The analysis code and the collected data are publicly available.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Machine translation (MT) is routinely evaluated using various segment-level similarity metrics against one or more reference translations. At the same time, reference translations acquired in the standard way are often criticized for flaws of various types. For several high-resourced language pairs, MT quality reaches levels comparable to the quality of the reference translation [1,2], and MT sometimes even significantly surpasses humans in a particular evaluation setting [3]. Given this, one could conclude that state-of-the-art MT has reached the point where reference-based evaluation is no longer reliable and that we must resort to other methods (such as targeted expert evaluation of particular outputs), even though they are costly, subjective and possibly impossible to automate.

The narrow goal of this work is to allow an ‘‘extension of the expiry date’’ for reference-based evaluation methods. More broadly, we want to formulate a methodology for creating reference translations that avoid the often-observed deficiencies of ‘‘standard’’ or ‘‘professional’’ reference translations, be it multiple interfering phenomena, inappropriate expressions, ignorance of topic-focus articulation (information structure) or other abundant shortcomings in the translation, which indicate their authors' insensitivity to the topic itself, but above all to the source and target language. To this end, we introduce so-called optimal reference translations (ORT), intended to represent optimal (ideal or excellent) human translations (should they be the subject of a translation quality evaluation). We focus on document-level translation and evaluation, in line with current trends in MT research [4,5,6,7] and with this special issue of NLE. We hope that ORT will offer a new approach to the evaluation of excellent MT outputs by becoming a gold standard in the true sense of the word. Our work addresses the following questions:

- • How should future MT research be navigated for languages where the quality of MT is already very good?

- • Is it worth creating an expensive optimal reference translation to compare with MT?

- • If various groups of annotators evaluate optimal reference and standard translations, will they all recognize the difference in quality?

Our contributions are then:

- • a definition of optimal reference translation and an in-depth analysis of evaluations and of the relationship between evaluation and translation editing;

- • a reflection on what a high-quality translation means for different types of annotators;

- • publication of the Optimal Reference Translations of English \rightarrow Czech dataset, with a subset evaluated in the aforementioned manner.

After discussing related work (Section 2), we define ORT and describe its creation process (Section 3). Next, we describe our evaluation campaign of ORT: the data, the annotation interface, and the annotation instructions (Section 3.2). We then examine our data from a statistical perspective and measure how well automated metrics predict human ratings (e.g. Overall rating from Spelling, Style, Meaning, etc.) (Section 4), paying special attention to predicting document-level ratings from segment-level ones. In the penultimate Section 5, we provide a detailed qualitative analysis of the human annotations, and we then discuss this work in the broader perspective of human evaluation of translations (Section 6). The analysis code and collected data are publicly available.
